title: The ravens (1 Kings 17:1–6)
hookLine: in drought, ravens bring Elijah bread and meat

cards: No family tree. No birth story. No call scene.
Just a name and a place: Elijah the Tishbite, of the settlers of Gilead. He stands before King Ahab and says there will be no dew or rain in these years, except by his word. Then he leaves.
God sends him to hide by a brook near the Jordan, in a land about to go dry. And the food that keeps him alive there comes from a source nobody would have picked.

teach.b: God tells Elijah to hide by the brook Cherith. In the 1917 Jewish translation: "thou shalt drink of the brook; and I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there." And they do.
"And the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook."

teach.h: ORVIM: RAVENS, ON THE TORAH'S LIST.
teach.b: The Hebrew word is orvim, ravens. Of all birds.

teach.h: THE PROPHET HAS TO BE FED.
teach.b: In the Torah's list of birds Israel may not eat, the raven is there by name, and here it is carrying bread and meat to a prophet, morning and evening, in a drought.
Some later commentators wondered whether orvim might mean people instead of birds.
The plain story keeps the birds, and keeps the strangeness: help arrives on the wings of something the Torah set apart as unfit for the table. There's a quieter point too.
Elijah has just spoken a drought into the land, and the very next thing the text shows is that he has to be fed.
He sits by a brook, waits, and accepts food from birds.

teach.h: THE RAVENS BROUGHT HIM BREAD AND FLESH.
teach.b: After his big word, the prophet's next scene is about receiving. And it doesn't last: after a while, the text says, the brook dried up, because there had been no rain, and he'll have to move on.
But for a time the help came, twice a day, from the last place he'd have looked.

how: Jews read Elijah's story in the book of Kings, and Elijah appears in Jewish practice beyond it, as in the cup of Elijah set out at the Passover seder.

practice: Remember a time someone helped you whom you didn't expect, a stranger, someone you had written off, someone you'd kept at arm's length, and let that face stay a moment.
Then ask whether help is being offered today that you're refusing because of where it comes from. If you pray, you can give thanks for the ravens in your life.
